claim: Embryonic growth occurs predominately by an increase in cell number.
source: Embryonic growth occurs predominately by an increase in cell number; little is known about growth mechanisms later in development when fibrous tissues account for the bulk of adult vertebrate mass.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The number of collagen fibrils increases during embryonic development and then remains constant during postnatal growth.
source: We show that the number of collagen fibrils increases during embryonic development and then remains constant during postnatal growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 2D and Table 1 showing fibril counts at different developmental stages.

claim: Embryonic growth was explained predominately by increases in fibril number and length.
source: Embryonic growth was explained predominately by increases in fibril number and length.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 2D showing increases in fibril number and Figure 7—figure supplement 2 showing increases in fibril length during embryonic development.

claim: Postnatal growth arose predominately from increases in fibril length and diameter.
source: Postnatal growth arose predominately from increases in fibril length and diameter.
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 2 showing increases in fibril diameter and estimates of fibril length during postnatal development.

claim: A helical crimp structure was established in embryogenesis and persisted postnatally.
source: A helical crimp structure was established in embryogenesis, and persisted postnatally.
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstructions shown in Figure 7 demonstrating helical crimp structure at different developmental stages.

claim: The shape and size of tendon is determined by the number and position of embryonic fibroblasts.
source: The data support a model where the shape and size of tendon is determined by the number and position of embryonic fibroblasts.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data showing stable cell-cell contacts and fibril bundle numbers established during embryonic development.

claim: The collagen fibrils that embryonic cells synthesise provide a template for postnatal growth by structure-based matrix expansion.
source: The collagen fibrils that these cells synthesise provide a template for postnatal growth by structure-based matrix expansion.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the observation that fibril numbers remain constant postnatally while fibril diameter increases uniformly throughout the ECM.

claim: Tendons transmit tensile forces from muscles to bone.
source: Tendons transmit tensile forces from muscles to bone and are amongst the heaviest loaded tissues in vertebrates; the forces have been estimated at ∼ 16 kN/Kg of body mass (Harrison et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harrison et al., 2010.

claim: Forces in tendons have been estimated at approximately 16 kN/Kg of body mass.
source: Tendons transmit tensile forces from muscles to bone and are amongst the heaviest loaded tissues in vertebrates; the forces have been estimated at ∼ 16 kN/Kg of body mass (Harrison et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harrison et al., 2010.

claim: The ability of tendons to transmit large forces is directly attributable to an extracellular matrix comprising collagen fibrils aligned parallel to the tissue long axis.
source: The ability of tendons to transmit such large forces is directly attributable to an extracellular matrix (ECM) comprising collagen fibrils aligned parallel to the tissue long axis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field about tendon structure-function relationships.

claim: Scleraxis (Scx) transformed studies of tendon development.
source: The discovery of Scleraxis (Scx), amongst all other transcription factors, transformed studies of tendon development (Brent et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brent et al., 2003.

claim: The generation of Scx-GFP mice showed the precise location of tendons in the proximal–distal axis of the limb.
source: The generation of Scx-GFP mice showed the precise location of tendons in the proximal–distal axis of the limb (Schweitzer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schweitzer et al., 2001.

claim: Scx specifies important interactions between somatic muscle and cartilage cell lineages leading to tendon development.
source: Scx specifies important interactions between somatic muscle and cartilage cell lineages leading to tendon development (Brent et al., 2003; Sugimoto et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brent et al., 2003 and Sugimoto et al., 2013a.

claim: Scx is also expressed in non-tendon tissues including ligaments, intervertebral discs, joints, and cartilage around the chondro-tendinous/ligamentous junction.
source: However, Scx is also expressed in non-tendon tissues including ligaments, intervertebral discs, joints, and cartilage around the chondro-tendinous/ligamentous junction (Sugimoto et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sugimoto et al., 2013b.

claim: Tenomodulin is expressed in tendons and ligaments and is a regulator of tenocyte proliferation and is involved in collagen fibril maturation.
source: Tenomodulin, a type II transmembrane glycoprotein, is expressed in tendons and ligaments and is a regulator of tenocyte proliferation and is involved in collagen fibril maturation (Docheva et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Docheva et al., 2005.

claim: Mohawk, EGR1, and EGR2 are transcription factors involved in tendon formation.
source: Further studies have shown that Mohawk (Liu et al., 2010), EGR1, and EGR2 are transcription factors that are also involved in tendon formation (Lejard et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2010 and Lejard et al., 2011.

claim: The ability of EGR1 to promote tendon differentiation is partially mediated by TGFβ2.
source: Furthermore, the ability of EGR1 to promote tendon differentiation is partially mediated by TGFβ2 (Guerquin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guerquin et al., 2013.

claim: Two main signalling pathways, TGFβ and FGF, have been identified in vertebrate tendon development.
source: Two main signalling pathways, TGFβ and FGF, have been identified in vertebrate tendon development (Maeda et al., 2011, and for review see Tozer and Duprez, 2005; Schweitzer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maeda et al., 2011, Tozer and Duprez, 2005, and Schweitzer et al., 2010.

claim: Collagen type I occurs in virtually all fibrous tissues along with type III, V, XII, XIV, fibronectin and small proteoglycans such as decorin.
source: Collagen type I occurs in virtually all fibrous tissues along with type III, V (Birk and Mayne, 1997), XII, XIV (Ansorge et al., 2009), fibronectin and small proteoglycans such as decorin (Berenson et al., 1996; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Birk and Mayne, 1997; Ansorge et al., 2009; Berenson et al., 1996; and Zhang et al., 2006.

claim: The defining event that signifies the onset of functional tendon development is the appearance of collagen fibrils in the ECM.
source: The defining event that signifies the onset of functional tendon development is the appearance of collagen fibrils in the ECM.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field of tendon development.

claim: The distribution of collagen fibril diameters distinguishes two stages in tendon development.
source: The distribution of collagen fibril diameters distinguishes two stages in tendon development.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 2 showing unimodal distribution in embryonic tendon and bimodal distribution in postnatal tendon.

claim: In mouse, stage 1 begins at E12.5 when narrow (∼35 nm) diameter collagen fibrils are formed within actin-dependent fibripositors at the cell surface.
source: In mouse, stage 1 begins at E12.5 when narrow (∼35 nm) diameter collagen fibrils are formed within actin-dependent fibripositors at the cell surface (Canty et al., 2004, 2006; Kalson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Canty et al., 2004, 2006 and Kalson et al., 2013.

claim: During embryonic tendon development, the length and width of the tissue doubles in a few days, accompanied by two-orders of magnitude increases in elastic modulus and ultimate tensile strength.
source: The length and width of the tissue doubles in a few days, and is accompanied by two-orders of magnitude increases in elastic modulus and ultimate tensile strength (McBride et al., 1985, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McBride et al., 1985, 1988.

claim: Serial section transmission electron microscopy of chick embryonic tendon showed that the tendon matrix contains bundles of collagen fibrils that undergo gradual rotation over several microns.
source: Serial section transmission electron microscopy (ss-TEM) of chick embryonic tendon showed that the tendon matrix contains bundles of collagen fibrils that undergo gradual rotation over several microns (Birk and Trelstad, 1986; Birk et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Birk and Trelstad, 1986 and Birk et al., 1989.

claim: The collagen fibril bundles are stabilised by cell–cell connections containing cadherin-11.
source: Moreover, the collagen fibril bundles are stabilised by cell–cell connections containing cadherin-11 (Richardson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richardson et al., 2007.

claim: During stage 1 there is a modest increase in fibril diameter (to ∼40 nm), which has been replicated in vitro by slow stretching of a 3-dimensional tendon-like construct containing embryonic tenocytes.
source: During stage 1 there is a modest increase in fibril diameter (to ∼40 nm), which has been replicated in vitro by slow stretching of a 3-dimensional (3D) tendon-like construct containing embryonic tenocytes (Kalson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalson et al., 2011.

claim: At birth (in the mouse), the unimodal distribution of narrow fibrils is quickly (within a few days) replaced by a bimodal distribution of fibril diameters with a range of 35–400 nm.
source: At birth (in the mouse), the unimodal distribution of narrow fibrils is quickly (within a few days) replaced by a bimodal distribution of fibril diameters with a range of 35–400 nm (Goh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goh et al., 2012 and data in Figure 2.

claim: The transition from unimodal to bimodal distributions specifies the onset of stage 2.
source: The transition from unimodal to bimodal distributions specifies the onset of stage 2.
evidence: This is a definition based on the observed changes in fibril diameter distributions.

claim: Crimp becomes evident early in embryonic development and provides the biomechanically important 'toe-region' to the force–extension curve.
source: Crimp becomes evident early in embryonic development (Shah et al., 1982) and provides the biomechanically important 'toe-region' to the force–extension curve (Shah et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shah et al., 1982.

claim: Mathematical modelling of crimped collagen fibrils in tendon suggests crimp to be helical in structure.
source: Crimp structure has been investigated by plane polarised light microscopy and by SEM (Raspanti et al., 2005; Franchi et al., 2007), but the structure of crimp is still debated; numerous studies describe a planar 2D undulating crimp, but mathematical modelling of crimped collagen fibrils in tendon suggests crimp to be helical in structure (Grytz and Meschke, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grytz and Meschke, 2009.

claim: At E15.5 the vast majority of collagen fibrils had near-circular outlines and were therefore perpendicular (to a close approximation) to the tendon long axis.
source: The results showed that at E15.5 the vast majority of collagen fibrils had near-circular outlines and were therefore perpendicular (to a close approximation) to the tendon long axis.
evidence: This is based on TEM observations of transverse sections as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At E15.5, collagen fibrils were organised in small groups termed 'fibril bundles' that occurred in channels defined by the plasma membranes of surrounding cells.
source: The fibrils were organised in small groups, which occurred in channels defined by the plasma membranes of surrounding cells. These groups of fibrils are termed 'fibril bundles' (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on TEM observations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At E15.5, collagen fibrils are being synthesised in fibripositors at the cell-matrix interface.
source: At this stage of development the collagen fibrils are being synthesised in fibripositors at the cell-matrix interface (Kalson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalson et al., 2013 and observation of fibripositors in Figure 1A.

claim: At birth the number of fibril profiles in fibril bundles increases >fourfold compared to E15.5.
source: At birth the number of fibril profiles in fibril bundles increases >fourfold, and the fibril bundles are well defined by cellular plasma membrane extensions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D and TEM images in Figure 1B.

claim: TEM images showed electron dense cell–cell junctions between adjacent cell membrane extensions.
source: TEM images showed electron dense cell–cell junctions between adjacent cell membrane extensions (Waggett et al., 2006; Richardson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Waggett et al., 2006 and Richardson et al., 2007, and observations in Figure 1B.

claim: In 6 weeks postnatal tendon, fibril bundles have grown in lateral size and are separated by elongated cell processes.
source: In 6 weeks postnatal tendon, fibril bundles have grown in lateral size and are separated by striking elongated cell processes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on TEM observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mean fibril diameter increased from 35.4 nm ± 0.2 nm at E15.5, to 46.5 ± 1.1 nm at birth and 160.1 ± 3.4 nm at 6 weeks postnatal.
source: Analysis of TEM images demonstrated that fibril diameter increased during development, with mean fibril diameter increasing from 35.4 nm ± 0.2 nm at E15.5, to 46.5 ± 1.1 nm at birth and 160.1 ± 3.4 nm at 6 weeks postnatal (Table 1, Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements presented in Table 1 and Figure 2A-C.

claim: A bimodal distribution of diameters was found in 6 week postnatal tendon.
source: A bimodal distribution of diameters was found in 6 week postnatal tendon, as previously described (Parry et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2C and citation to Parry et al., 1978.

claim: The increase in fibril diameter occurred uniformly throughout the ECM, and was not confined to fibrils close to the cell.
source: Notably, the increase in fibril diameter occurred uniformly throughout the ECM, and was not confined to fibrils close to the cell.
evidence: This is an observation from TEM images that is critical to understanding the mechanism of fibril growth.

claim: Approximately 700 fibrils were found in each fibril bundle at birth and also at 6 weeks postnatal.
source: After birth the number of fibrils stabilised; approximately 700 fibrils were found in each fibril bundle at birth and also at 6 weeks postnatal (Figure 2D, p = >0.1, Data in Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: The number of fibril bundles per nucleus was constant between newborn and 6 weeks (7.4 ± 0.3 bundles per cell vs 7.3 ± 0.3).
source: At the same time as the number of fibril profiles per bundle had stabilised the number of fibril bundles per nucleus was also constant (7.4 ± 0.3 bundles per cell vs 7.3 ± 0.3 in newborn vs 6 week, p = >0.1, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E with statistical analysis.

claim: Fibripositors were absent from 6 week tail tendon.
source: Fibripositors (sites of fibril formation during stage 1) were absent from 6 week tail tendon.
evidence: This is an observation from TEM images of 6 week tendon.

claim: The number of fibril profiles per μm2 fell by a factor of ∼10 during development as the diameter of the fibrils increased.
source: The number of fibril profiles per μm2 fell by a factor of ∼10 during development as the diameter of the fibrils increased (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Fibril area fraction (FAF) increased during development from 1.4 ± 0.3% at E15.5, to 17.6 ± 1.3% at newborn, to 76.4 ± 1.3% at 6 weeks.
source: fibril area fraction (FAF) increased during development from 1.4 ± 0.3% at E15.5, to 17.6 ± 1.3% at newborn, to 76.4 ± 1.3% at 6 weeks (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2G and Table 1.

claim: The mean fibril area increased from 1006.5 ± 13.8 nm2 at E15.5, to 2137.9 ± 370.9 nm2 at newborn to 24,606.8 ± 933.0 nm2 at 6 weeks.
source: Corresponding with increase in fibril diameter, the mean fibril area increased from 1006.5 ± 13.8 nm2 at E15.5, to 2137.9 ± 370.9 nm2 at newborn to 24,606.8 ± 933.0 nm2 at 6 weeks (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2H and Table 1.

claim: At E15.5, cells are rounded and close together.
source: The cells at E15.5 are rounded and close together.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cell bodies move apart as fibril bundles increase in size, eventually becoming star shaped (in transverse section) at 6 weeks postnatal.
source: The cell bodies move apart as fibril bundles increase in size, eventually becoming star shaped (in transverse section) at 6 weeks postnatal.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cells are stacked on top of each other, maintaining the precise longitudinal alignment of the fibril bundles.
source: Longitudinal views (B and C) show the close relationship of cells, which are stacked on top of each other, thereby maintaining the precise longitudinal alignment of the fibril bundles.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: In newborn and 6 week tendon the fibril bundles had a regular wavy configuration (crimp).
source: Reconstructing the fibril bundles in three dimensions (in red in Figure 3C) showed that in newborn and 6 week tendon the fibril bundles had a regular wavy configuration (crimp).
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cell body length decreased during development from 60 ± 2 μm at E15.5, to 55 ± 3 μm at birth, to 27 ± 2 μm at 6 weeks.
source: Cell body length decreased during development from 60 ± 2 μm at E15.5, to 55 ± 3 μm at birth, to 27 ± 2 μm at 6 weeks (Data in Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SBF-SEM reconstructions.

claim: Cell volume remains relatively constant during postnatal matrix growth between newborn and 6 weeks.
source: Calculation of cell dimensions demonstrated that cell volume remains relatively constant during this period of matrix growth between newborn and 6 weeks (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cell surface area increases greatly during postnatal development due to the growth of long cell processes.
source: but the cell surface area increases greatly due to the growth of these long processes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: When isolated from tendon and plated on plastic, tendon cells become flat and have the characteristic appearance of a fibroblast in culture.
source: When isolated from tendon and plated on plastic the cell shape changed radically: in 2D cell culture the cells become flat and have the characteristic appearance of a fibroblast in culture (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on light microscopy observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no difference in the surface area of the cells when cultured on plastic comparing E15.5 cells and 6 week cells.
source: There was no difference in the surface area of the cells when cultured on plastic comparing E15.5 cells and 6 week cells (Data in Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The number of cells per unit volume of tendon tissue fell significantly from 1.26 ± 0.02 to 0.91 ± 0.02 cells per 1000 µm3 between E15.5 and birth, to 0.14 ± 0.01 at 6 weeks.
source: The number of cells per unit volume of tendon tissue fell significantly from 1.26 ± 0.02 to 0.91 ± 0.02 cells per 1000 µm3 between E15.5 and birth, to 0.14 ± 0.01 at 6 weeks (p = <0.05, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SBF-SEM reconstructions shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cells per unit area of transverse tendon area showed a significant fall from 30.1 ± 0.6 cells per 1000 µm2 (E.15.5) to 20.5 ± 0.8 (newborn) to 1.9 ± 0.1 (6 week).
source: Measurement of cells per unit area of transverse tendon area showed a significant fall from 30.1 ± 0.6 cells per 1000 µm2 (E.15.5) to 20.5 ± 0.8 (newborn) to 1.9 ± 0.1 (6 week, p = <0.05, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At birth cell nuclei were spaced 39.9 ± 1.8 µm apart (on the longitudinal axis) and at 6-weeks they were 27.5 ± 1.1 µm apart.
source: At birth cell nuclei were spaced 39.9 ± 1.8 µm apart (on the longitudinal axis) and at 6-weeks they were 27.5 ± 1.1 µm apart (p = <0.05, Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The discrepancy between cell length and distance between nuclei in newborn tissue was due to overlap of cells in stacks.
source: The discrepancy between cell length and distance between nuclei in newborn tissue was due to overlap of cells in stacks (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on observations from 3D reconstructions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is a relative increase in the number of cells in longitudinal axis in cell channels during tendon growth comparing newborn with 6 week tendon.
source: These data suggest that there is a relative increase in the number of cells in longitudinal axis in cell channels during tendon growth comparing newborn with 6 week tendon.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on cell spacing and overlap.

claim: The horizontal distance between cell nuclei increased from 6.2 ± 0.2 to 31.5 ± 0.9 µm from birth to 6 weeks.
source: The horizontal distance between cell nuclei increased from 6.2 ± 0.2 to 31.5 ± 0.9 µm from birth to 6 weeks (p = <0.05, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 5F.

claim: At E15.5 no distinct cell membrane channels were formed via membrane protrusions contacting adjacent cells.
source: At E15.5 no distinct cell membrane channels were formed via membrane protrusions contacting adjacent cells; instead groups of narrow-diameter fibrils were seen between adjacent cell membranes or enclosed in cell membrane invaginations (as shown in Figures 1A, 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, data in Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on observations from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Newborn tenocytes formed protrusions that contacted adjacent cells and formed channels surrounding fibril bundles.
source: Newborn tenocytes formed protrusions that contacted adjacent cells; these formed channels surrounding fibril bundles (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on observations from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At 6 weeks a similar morphology of cell–cell contact was found as in newborn, although the cell processes were much longer.
source: At 6 weeks a similar morphology of cell–cell contact was found, although the cell processes were much longer (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on observations from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining revealed positive immunolocalisation of connexins 32 and 43 in mature (6 week) tendon.
source: Furthermore, immunofluorescence staining against connexins 32 and 43 revealed positive immunolocalisation of cell–cell junctions in mature (6 week) tendon (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: In newborn tendon each tendon cell forms distinct channel-defining protrusions that contact, on average, 4.6 ± 0.1 adjacent cells.
source: Quantitation of cell–cell contacts showed that in newborn tendon each tendon cell forms distinct channel-defining protrusions that contact, on average, 4.6 ± 0.1 adjacent cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SBF-SEM reconstructions shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At 6 weeks each tendon cell contacts 4.5 ± 0.1 adjacent cells.
source: At 6 weeks each tendon cell contacts 4.5 ± 0.1 adjacent cells (p = >0.05, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SBF-SEM reconstructions shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The number of protrusions per cell that contacted adjacent cells was similar in newborn and 6 week tendon (8.2 ± 0.2 vs 8.3 ± 0.2).
source: The number of protrusions per cell that contacted adjacent cells was also similar in newborn and 6 week tendon (8.2 ± 0.2 vs 8.3 ± 0.2, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from SBF-SEM reconstructions shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: At E15.5 an undulation or wavy pattern is seen in fibril bundles, but is neither regular nor well defined.
source: At E15.5 an undulation or wavy pattern is seen, but is neither regular nor well defined.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7B.

claim: By birth the fibril bundles have developed regular undulations, of defined and consistent wavelength.
source: By birth the fibril bundles have developed regular undulations, of defined and consistent wavelength.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The undulations in fibril bundles are in axial-register in newborn tendon.
source: Importantly the undulations are in axial-register (see Figure 7B, middle panel).
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The crimp structure derives from a helical spring sub-structure, and is not simply a planar (2D) undulation.
source: These data show the crimp to derive from a helical spring sub-structure, and is not simply a planar (2D) undulation.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7C demonstrating the spiral nature of crimp.

claim: The wavelength of the crimp increases during development from 14 ± 0.3 μm at birth to 99 ± 2.5 μm at 6 weeks.
source: The wavelength of the crimp increases during development from 14 ± 0.3 μm at birth to 99 ± 2.5 μm at 6 weeks (Table 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Data in Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SBF-SEM shown in Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The crimp helix radius was 1.6 ± 0.1 μm at birth and 2.3 ± 0.1 at 6 weeks.
source: The crimp helix radius (the distance from the central axis) was 1.6 ± 0.1 μm at birth and 2.3 ± 0.1 at 6 weeks.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements from SBF-SEM shown in Table 1.

claim: Tail length increased from 6.1 ± 0.3 mm (E15.5) to 10.9 ± 0.9 mm (newborn) to 67.6 ± 0.3 mm (6 week); overall a factor of 10 increase.
source: Tail length increased from 6.1 ± 0.3 mm (E15.5) to 10.9 ± 0.9 mm (newborn) to 67.6 ± 0.3 mm (6 week); overall a factor of 10 increase.
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: The increase in tail length between newborn and 6 weeks closely matches the change in crimp wavelength (∼factor of 6–7 fold increase).
source: The increase in length between newborn and 6 weeks closely matches the change in crimp wavelength (∼factor of 6–7 fold increase).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the data for tail length and crimp wavelength.

claim: In 119 out of 120 specimens examined, the helical coil turns in a left-handed spiral.
source: In 119 out of 120 specimens we have so far examined we have consistently found the helical coil to turn in a left-handed spiral.
evidence: This is based on observations from multiple SBF-SEM reconstructions.

claim: In one specimen from 6 week mouse a right-handed helix was observed.
source: In one specimen from 6 week mouse we observed a right-handed helix.
evidence: This is based on observation from one SBF-SEM reconstruction.

claim: The alternating handedness continues from polypeptide chains (left-handed helix), to collagen molecules (right-handed), to microfibrils (left-handed) and collagen fibrils (right-handed).
source: This continues the alternating handedness from polypeptide chains (left-handed helix), to collagen molecules (right-handed), to microfibrils (left-handed) and collagen fibrils (right-handed, as described in [Holmes et al., 2001]).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and citation to Holmes et al., 2001.

claim: The fibrils in tendon bundles form a left-handed helical macrostructure.
source: These data show that the fibrils in tendon bundles then form a left-handed helical macrostructure.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7.

claim: The left-handed spiral structure of fibril bundles has been observed in all anatomically distinct tendons examined using SBF-SEM, including mouse Achilles tendon and chick metatarsal tendons.
source: We have observed this left-handed spiral structure of fibril bundles in all the anatomically distinct tendons we have examined using SBF-SEM, including mouse Achilles tendon and chick metatarsal tendons, with different biomechanical properties compared with mouse-tail tendon, an axial tendon (Benjamin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on observations from multiple SBF-SEM studies and citation to Benjamin et al., 2008.

claim: Mean fibril length increased significantly from 125 ± 18 µm at E15.5, to 578 ± 17 µm in newborn tendon.
source: This demonstrated a significant increase in fibril length through development, from 125 ± 18 µm at E15.5, to 578 ± 17 µm in newborn tendon (Figure 7—figure supplement 2, p = <0.05, Data in Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by fibril tracking data from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: At E15.5, 160 fibril tips were identified within 10,000 µm fibril lengths tracked.
source: At E15.5 160 fibril tips were identified (within 10,000 µm fibril lengths tracked).
evidence: This is based on fibril tracking from SBF-SEM data.

claim: In newborn mouse tendon, 69 tips were found over ∼20,000 µm fibril lengths tracked.
source: In newborn mouse tendon, 69 tips were found (over ∼20,000 µm fibril lengths tracked).
evidence: This is based on fibril tracking from SBF-SEM data.

claim: At 6 weeks, 16 tips were identified within 10,000 µm fibril lengths tracked, all occurring in fibrils less than 150 nm in diameter.
source: At 6 weeks fibril tips were rare; 16 tips were identified within 10,000 µm fibril lengths tracked, all occurring in fibrils less than 150 nm in diameter (the smaller population of postnatal fibrils).
evidence: This is based on fibril tracking from SBF-SEM data.

claim: No fibril tips were found in fibrils >150 nm in diameter at 6 weeks.
source: No tips were found in fibrils >150 nm in diameter.
evidence: This is based on fibril tracking from SBF-SEM data.

claim: The estimated mean-length of fibrils less than 150 nm diameter at 6 weeks is 1250 ± 305 µm.
source: This gave an estimate of mean-length of 1250 ± 305 µm for fibrils less than 150 nm diameter.
evidence: This is calculated from fibril tracking data from SBF-SEM.

claim: Tendon development occurs in a two-stage process.
source: In conclusion, we have shown that tendon development occurs in a two-stage process.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In stage 1 the organisation of fibroblasts and the cellular channels for fibril deposition and growth are established, and cell-mediated control of collagen fibril deposition occurs.
source: In stage 1 the organisation of fibroblasts and the cellular channels for fibril deposition and growth are established, and cell-mediated control of collagen fibril deposition occurs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing fibril formation in fibripositors and establishment of cell-cell contacts during embryonic development.

claim: Stage 1 sets the developmental template for structure-based matrix expansion of the existing matrix in stage 2.
source: This sets the developmental template for structure-based matrix expansion of the existing matrix in stage 2, which drives the increase in the size of the matrix that underpins tissue growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that fibril numbers remain constant postnatally while fibrils grow in diameter and length.

claim: The cell-regulated number of cell processes define the boundaries of collagen fibril bundles and help to maintain the tramline organization of cells in the mature tissue.
source: Important features include the cell-regulated number of cell processes that define the boundaries of collagen fibril bundles and help to maintain the tramline organization of cells in the mature tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing stable numbers of cell-cell contacts and fibril bundles per cell during postnatal development.

claim: These mechanisms could be a paradigm for the growth of other matrix-rich tissues that are abundant in collagen fibrils.
source: These mechanisms could be a paradigm for the growth of other matrix-rich tissues that are abundant in collagen fibrils.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The close association of cells with bundles suggests that the cell shape strongly influences the configuration of the crimp structure.
source: The close association of cells with bundles suggests that the cell shape strongly influences the configuration of the crimp structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed close relationship between cell shape and fibril bundle crimp shown in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: Cell force generated by the actin-myosin system can create a crimp structure.
source: This is consistent with studies suggesting that cell force generated by the actin-myosin system can create a crimp structure (Herchenhan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Herchenhan et al., 2012.

claim: The length increase of the mouse-tail from newborn to 6 weeks by a factor of ∼6.2× closely matches the increase in crimp wavelength of ∼7.1×.
source: The length increase of the mouse-tail from newborn to 6 weeks by a factor of ∼6.2× closely matches the increase in crimp wavelength of ∼7.1×.
evidence: This is based on comparison of tail length and crimp wavelength measurements from Table 1.

claim: The close match between tail length increase and crimp wavelength increase suggests a simple crimp elongation process in synchrony with bundle and tissue elongation.
source: This suggests a simple crimp elongation process in synchrony with bundle and tissue elongation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between tail length and crimp wavelength increases.

claim: Fibril fusion is regulated by the directionality of collagen molecules in the fibril, the availability of tips from unipolar fibrils, and by the presence of proteoglycans at the fibril surface.
source: Thus, fibril fusion is regulated by the directionality of collagen molecules in the fibril (Kadler et al., 1990), the availability of tips from unipolar fibrils (Graham et al., 2000), and by the presence of proteoglycans at the fibril surface (Birk et al., 1995; Graham et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kadler et al., 1990; Graham et al., 2000; and Birk et al., 1995.

claim: An important consequence of fibril fusion is the inevitable reduction in fibril numbers as fibrils fuse together, and the decrease in the number of fibrils per cell.
source: An important and often overlooked consequence of fibril fusion is the inevitable reduction in fibril numbers as fibrils fuse together, and the decrease in the number of fibrils per cell.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of fibril fusion.

claim: Fibril fusion has no effect on fibril volume fraction as no new fibril volume is created by any type of fusion.
source: It is also to be noted that fibril fusion has no effect on fibril volume fraction as no new fibril volume is created by any type of fusion
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of fibril fusion.

claim: Very few fibril fusion (tip-shaft) events were found when fibrils were tracked with SBF-SEM.
source: we found very few fibril fusion (tip-shaft) events when we tracked fibrils with SBF-SEM.
evidence: This is based on observations from fibril tracking in SBF-SEM data.

claim: Collagen fibril numbers (in profile) increased during stage 1 of development and remained constant during stage 2, despite increases in fibril diameter.
source: The data presented here show that collagen fibril numbers (in profile) increased during stage 1 of development and remained constant during stage 2, despite increases in fibril diameter (in stage 1 and stage 2).
evidence: This is based on quantitative data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The diameter and fibril number data do not support shaft-to-shaft fusion as a major contributor to increases in fibril diameter during tendon development.
source: Although we cannot rule out tip-to-tip fusion (which would not be expected to affect fibril diameter) our diameter and fibril number data do not support shaft-to-shaft fusion as a major contributor to increases in fibril diameter during tendon development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fibril numbers remain constant while diameters increase.

claim: Irregularly shaped fibrils would be expected to occur if lateral fusion was occurring, but were not observed.
source: We also have not observed irregularly shaped fibrils, which would be expected to occur if lateral fusion was occurring.
evidence: This is based on observations from TEM and SBF-SEM images.

claim: In the surface-nucleation-and-propagation (SNP) model, collagen molecules accrete onto the growing tips of fibrils and to the molecular reversal region in bipolar fibrils.
source: An alternative mechanism of fibril growth is the surface-nucleation-and-propagation (SNP) model in which collagen molecules accrete onto the growing tips of fibrils (Holmes et al., 1992, 1998) and to the molecular reversal region in bipolar fibrils (Trotter et al., 1998, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holmes et al., 1992, 1998 and Trotter et al., 1998, 2000.

claim: The SNP model predicts that collagen fibrils have specific binding sites for collagen molecules, leading to growth in diameter and length.
source: The SNP model predicts that collagen fibrils have specific binding sites for collagen molecules, leading to growth in diameter and length.
evidence: This is a description of the SNP model based on cited literature.

claim: Fibril growth is determined by local structure at the fibril surface and is an example of interface-controlled growth as opposed to diffusion-limited accretion onto the fibril surface.
source: Thus, fibril growth is determined by local structure at the fibril surface and is an example of interface-controlled growth as opposed to diffusion-limited accretion onto the fibril surface.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the SNP model and the observation that fibril diameters are independent of distance from the cell.

claim: The occurrence of an abrupt limitation in fibril diameter at the growing tips of vertebrate collagen fibrils suggests a structure-based mechanism for fibril growth.
source: The occurrence of an abrupt limitation in fibril diameter at the growing tips of vertebrate collagen fibrils also suggests a structure-based mechanism for fibril growth (Holmes et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holmes et al., 1998.

claim: If collagen molecules could assemble onto non-specific binding sites on the fibril in an uncoordinated manner, the axial mass profiles would be expected to show pronounced random fluctuations.
source: If collagen molecules could assemble onto non-specific binding sites on the fibril in an uncoordinated manner, the axial mass profiles would be expected to show pronounced random fluctuations.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected if fibril growth was not structure-based.

claim: If collagen fibril growth was diffusion-limited, fibrils closer to the cell might be expected to have larger diameters because of the ready availability of collagen molecules emerging from the cell.
source: In the case of diffusion-limited growth, collagen fibrils closer to the cell might be expected to have larger diameters because of the ready availability of collagen molecules emerging from the cell.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected if fibril growth was diffusion-limited.

claim: As fibril diameters are independent of distance from the cell, it seems more likely that fibril growth (especially in postnatal tendon) is strongly influenced by the local structure of the fibril surface.
source: However, as fibril diameters are independent of distance from the cell, it seems more likely that fibril growth (especially in postnatal tendon) is strongly influenced by the local structure of the fibril surface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fibril diameters are uniform throughout the ECM.

claim: The establishment of fibril number during stage 1 of development and subsequent growth in fibril diameter during stage 2 by the SNP mechanism would explain the observed increase in fibril diameter in stage 2 and the lateral growth of the tissue.
source: Thus, the establishment of fibril number during stage 1 of development and subsequent growth in fibril diameter during stage 2 by the SNP mechanism (in the absence of overt shaft-to-shaft fibril fusion) would explain the observed increase in fibril diameter in stage 2 and the lateral growth of the tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating the data with the SNP model to explain tissue growth.

claim: Cells at E15.5 and newborn had convoluted profiles, were slender cylinders with overlapping ends, and were ∼50–60 µm in length.
source: As shown in Figure 4, cells at E15.5 and newborn had convoluted profiles, were slender cylinders with overlapping ends, and were ∼50–60 µm in length.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cells in 6 weeks postnatal tendon had prominent lateral cellular extensions that reached deep into the ECM, were short (∼25 µm) and stacked in rows on their blunt ends.
source: In contrast, cells in 6 weeks postnatal had prominent lateral cellular extensions that reached deep into the ECM, were short (∼25 µm) and stacked in rows on their blunt ends.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cells at 6 weeks postnatal tendon remained in contact with each other via their cellular extensions regardless of the distance between the cell bodies where the nucleus was located.
source: Importantly, cells at 6 weeks postnatal tendon remained in contact with each other via their cellular extensions regardless of the distance between the cell bodies where the nucleus was located.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: The main cell bodies move laterally apart because of the expansion of the ECM but maintain their longitudinal relationship, thereby generating the tramline organisation seen in mature tendon.
source: The data show that the main cell bodies move laterally apart because of the expansion of the ECM but maintain their longitudinal relationship, thereby generating the tramline organisation seen in mature tendon.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing increased lateral spacing of cells while maintaining longitudinal cell stacks.

claim: Crimp first appears during embryonic tendon development.
source: Crimp first appears during embryonic tendon development (Shah et al., 1982) but the mechanism of crimp formation remains unknown, largely because of the impracticalities of studying its formation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shah et al., 1982.

claim: The mechanism of crimp formation remains unknown.
source: Crimp first appears during embryonic tendon development (Shah et al., 1982) but the mechanism of crimp formation remains unknown, largely because of the impracticalities of studying its formation in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Whole tails were fixed without disturbing the axial attachment to the skeleton to preserve the tension in the tendon and avoid major changes in crimp structure.
source: In our studies we were careful to preserve the tension in the tendon, avoiding major changes in crimp structure (Shah et al., 1977), by fixing whole tails without disturbing the axial attachment to the skeleton.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used, with citation to Shah et al., 1977.

claim: No kinks were found in the crimp structure as previously described.
source: We found no kinks as previously described (Raspanti et al., 2005) but instead observed a left-handed spiral running the length of our 3D reconstructions.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7, contrasting with previous reports cited as Raspanti et al., 2005.

claim: Fibril bundles are continuous over the distances measured, forming parallel spirals in axial register to provide uniform biomechanical properties when loaded.
source: It is important to note that fibril bundles are continuous over the distances we have measured here, forming parallel spirals in axial register to provide uniform biomechanical properties when loaded, and there is a close relationship between the cell and the fibril bundle.
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstructions from SBF-SEM shown in Figure 7.
